concepts.name: Replacement of 'Internal Disturbance' with 'Armed Rebellion' as grounds for National Emergency
key_dimensions: Original Article 352 language vs. post-44th Amendment language and why the change matters
Narrowing the scope: how 'armed rebellion' is harder to invoke than 'internal disturbance'
UPSC trap: distinguishing between the three grounds — war, external aggression, armed rebellion
Comparison with 42nd Amendment which had broadened emergency powers — 44th as corrective measure

concepts.name: Cabinet's Written Recommendation as a Precondition for Proclamation of National Emergency
key_dimensions: Constitutional provision: Article 352(3) — written communication by Union Cabinet (not just PM)
Pre-44th Amendment gap: President could act on PM's oral advice, enabling abuse (1975 precedent)
UPSC trap: 'Cabinet' here means Union Cabinet collectively, not just PM or Council of Ministers
Significance in preventing unilateral executive action by a single authority

concepts.name: Special Majority Requirement for Parliamentary Approval of National Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 352(6): approval by special majority — majority of total membership AND 2/3 of members present and voting
Time limit: must be approved within one month of proclamation (reduced from two months by 44th Amendment)
UPSC trap: distinguishing this special majority from Constitutional Amendment majority under Article 368
Contrast with revocation procedure — simple majority suffices for revocation

concepts.name: Lok Sabha's Exclusive Power to Revoke National Emergency via Simple Majority
key_dimensions: Article 352(8): President must revoke if Lok Sabha passes resolution by simple majority
Special session mechanism: 1/10th of total Lok Sabha members can requisition a special sitting
UPSC trap: Rajya Sabha has NO role in revocation — asymmetry between approval and revocation
Democratic significance: lower house representing people's will as ultimate check on executive

concepts.name: Periodic Renewal Requirement for Continuation of National Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 352(4): every six months renewal requires fresh approval by special majority in both Houses
Pre-44th Amendment: no mandatory renewal — Emergency of 1975 continued without fresh approval
UPSC trap: initial approval is one month; renewal is every six months — different time frames
Practical implication: Parliament must continuously justify continuation, preventing indefinite emergency

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Proclamation of National Emergency
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment restored justiciability — courts can review if proclamation is mala fide or irrelevant
Minerva Mills (1980) and subsequent cases affirming judicial review of emergency proclamations
UPSC trap: 38th Amendment (1975) had made satisfaction of President non-justiciable — 44th reversed this
Limits of judicial review: courts examine procedural compliance and relevance, not adequacy of grounds

concepts.name: Protection of Fundamental Rights During National Emergency — Article 19 Suspension Limits
key_dimensions: Article 358 amended: suspension of Article 19 only during war or external aggression, NOT armed rebellion
Pre-44th Amendment: Article 19 suspended automatically during any National Emergency
UPSC trap: Article 19 suspension (Art. 358) vs. suspension of enforcement of other FRs (Art. 359) — different mechanisms
Laws made inconsistent with Article 19 during armed rebellion emergency remain challengeable

concepts.name: Article 359 and Restriction on Suspension of Articles 20 and 21 During Emergency
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment: Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even by Presidential order under Article 359
Pre-44th Amendment: President could suspend enforcement of ALL fundamental rights including right to life
UPSC trap: Article 359 suspends 'enforcement' (right to move court), not the rights themselves — Article 358 actually suspends Article 19
ADM Jabalpur case (1976) and how 44th Amendment was a direct legislative response to that judgment

concepts.name: Safeguards Against Misuse of President's Rule (Article 356) — 44th Amendment Changes
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment: President's Rule must be approved by Parliament within two months (no change here, but reinforced)
S.R. Bommai case (1994) as judicial complement to 44th Amendment's spirit on floor test requirement
UPSC trap: 44th Amendment itself had limited direct changes to Art. 356 — most safeguards came via judicial interpretation
Rajya Sabha's role in President's Rule approval vs. its lack of role in National Emergency revocation

concepts.name: Separation of National Emergency Proclamation into State-Specific vs. All-India Application
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment: Article 352 allows proclamation limited to a specific part/state of India
Pre-44th Amendment: Emergency proclamation was necessarily nationwide in application
UPSC trap: even a state-specific National Emergency must follow the same special majority approval procedure
Significance: prevents disproportionate response — targeted application reduces democratic disruption

concepts.name: The 1975 Emergency as the Foundational Context for 44th Amendment Safeguards
key_dimensions: How 42nd Amendment (1976) had concentrated power — 44th Amendment as deliberate reversal
Shah Commission Report findings and their link to specific 44th Amendment provisions
UPSC trap: 44th Amendment passed in 1978 under Janata government — not during Emergency itself
Specific abuses of 1975 (oral advice of PM, no Cabinet recommendation) mapped to specific 44th Amendment provisions

concepts.name: Distinction Between 44th Amendment Changes to Article 352 vs. Article 356 vs. Article 360
key_dimensions: Article 352 (National Emergency): most extensively reformed by 44th Amendment
Article 360 (Financial Emergency): 44th Amendment made no significant changes — UPSC trap area
Article 356 (State Emergency): limited direct changes by 44th Amendment vs. extensive judicial safeguards
Comparative table: which emergency type got which safeguards — a classic UPSC differentiation question

concepts.name: Role of Election Commission and Right to Elections as Implied Safeguard
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment proposed (but Parliament did not ultimately enact) restoration of right to property as FR — context of emergency abuse
Provision that Lok Sabha and State Assembly terms cannot be extended beyond one year at a time during emergency
UPSC trap: Article 83(2) extension of Lok Sabha during emergency — maximum one year at a time, not unlimited
Democratic accountability mechanism: elections must occur within six months of emergency revocation

concepts.name: Restoration of Pre-42nd Amendment Position on Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment
key_dimensions: 42nd Amendment had placed Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights (Articles 31C expansion) — 44th partially reversed this
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down parts of 42nd Amendment that 44th had not yet corrected
UPSC trap: 44th Amendment and Minerva Mills judgment work in tandem — knowing which change came from statute vs. judiciary
Restoration of judicial review as fundamental to emergency safeguards — connecting FRs and emergency provisions

concepts.name: The Concept of 'Satisfaction of the President' and Its Reviewability After 44th Amendment
key_dimensions: Pre-44th: 38th Amendment made President's satisfaction final and non-justiciable
44th Amendment deleted clause making satisfaction non-justiciable, restoring courts' power to examine
UPSC trap: 'satisfaction of President' in Art. 352 means satisfaction of Council of Ministers — not personal satisfaction
Standard of judicial review: courts apply 'relevance and bona fide' test, not 'correctness' test

concepts.name: Notification and Communication Procedure Under Article 352 Post-44th Amendment
key_dimensions: Written communication requirement from Cabinet: prevents informal or verbal invocation
Role of Prime Minister vs. full Cabinet — collective responsibility dimension
UPSC trap: Article 352(3) says 'Union Cabinet' — this is the full cabinet, not Cabinet Committee or PM alone
Procedural vs. substantive safeguards — this is primarily a procedural safeguard against individual abuse

concepts.name: Impact of 44th Amendment on Centre-State Relations During Emergency
key_dimensions: During National Emergency, Parliament gains power to legislate on State List subjects — unchanged by 44th Amendment
Sarkaria Commission (1983) recommendations on Art. 356 as follow-up to 44th Amendment's incomplete reform of federalism
UPSC trap: 44th Amendment did NOT change Article 353 (effect of National Emergency on legislative powers)
Tension between emergency federalism and the 44th Amendment's democratic safeguards

concepts.name: 44th Amendment and the Right to Constitutional Remedies During Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 32 (right to move Supreme Court) cannot be suspended under Article 359 for violations of Articles 20 and 21
Pre-44th: ADM Jabalpur (1976) had held detention without trial unchallengeable — 44th Amendment overturned this legislatively
UPSC trap: Article 226 (High Court writs) can be restricted by Presidential order under Art. 359, but Article 32 for Arts. 20-21 cannot
Habeas corpus and the 44th Amendment — direct connection between emergency jurisprudence and the amendment

concepts.name: Comparison of Safeguards: National Emergency vs. Financial Emergency — What 44th Amendment Did and Did Not Change
key_dimensions: Financial Emergency (Art. 360): no enhanced safeguards added by 44th Amendment — never been proclaimed in India
National Emergency: comprehensive overhaul of approval, renewal, revocation, and grounds
UPSC trap: Financial Emergency requires simple majority approval — far lower threshold than National Emergency post-44th Amendment
Why Financial Emergency was left unreformed — political context of Janata government's priorities in 1977-79

concepts.name: Parliamentary Oversight Mechanisms Introduced by 44th Amendment as a System of Checks
key_dimensions: Aggregated view: written Cabinet advice + special majority approval + monthly/six-monthly renewal + Lok Sabha revocation power = layered checks
UPSC trap: identifying WHICH house has WHICH power — Lok Sabha alone revokes; both Houses approve; only Cabinet (not Parliament) initiates
Comparison with Westminster model and other democratic emergency frameworks
Practical effectiveness: whether these safeguards would actually prevent a recurrence of 1975-type emergency in current political context
